title: Seven Levels Agentic Prompt Formats

tactic.name: Master the Seven Agentic Prompt Formats
tactic.one_liner: The prompt is the fundamental unit of engineering — so stop writing one-off prompts and start building a library of reusable, consistently-structured agentic prompts assembled from a fixed set of swappable Lego-block sections, scaled level by level from a one-line ad-hoc prompt to a prompt that writes and improves your other prompts.
tactic.why_uncomfortable: It asks engineers to treat 'prompt engineering' — the skill that got mocked as a joke — as one of the most important engineering disciplines of the age of agents, and to invest real design effort into files that look trivially small. It also demands a mindset most engineers have not made: you are no longer writing prompts only for yourself. Every prompt now has three readers — you, your team, and your agents (the stakeholder trifecta) — and a single well-crafted prompt can generate tens or hundreds of hours of work while a single bad one compounds failure at the same rate. That leverage forces you to slow down, standardize, and template work you used to fire off casually.

mission: Level up your agentic prompt engineering by mastering seven reusable prompt formats and the ~13 composable sections that make them up, so you can consistently CRUD (create/read/update/delete) reusable prompts at light speed for the trifecta. Being able to reach for the right level — usually Level 3 or 4 — and swap in exactly the sections you need is what lets you hand more and more work to compute, move from inside-the-loop to outside-the-loop to ZTE, and achieve asymmetric engineering leverage in the age of agents.

stakeholder_trifecta.definition: The three audiences every agentic prompt is written for at once: You, Your Team, and Your Agents. Named 'the stakeholder trifecta for the age of agents.' A new consumer of your work has appeared — your agent — and prompts must communicate clearly to all three.
stakeholder_trifecta.you: Your future self returning to a prompt weeks later must instantly understand what it does. Consistent structure (collapse to H2s, read the top) makes that instant.
stakeholder_trifecta.team: A coworker must be able to pick up the prompt cold and run it top to bottom. Dan's test: 'If I handed this to a coworker, could they complete this work top to bottom? If that's true, you've probably written a high quality prompt.'
stakeholder_trifecta.agents: The most important reader. Powerful modern models reason over your prompt as a user prompt; consistent, information-dense sections reduce their confusion and let one prompt fire tens to hundreds of tool calls reliably for minutes to hours.
stakeholder_trifecta.dan_words: "We're now engineering for three audiences, you, your team, your agents. This is the stakeholder trifecta for the age of agents."

core_concepts.name: The prompt is the fundamental unit of engineering
core_concepts.plain_english: In the age of agents the prompt — not the function, not the file — is the atomic unit of engineering work. Because every line of an agentic prompt can trigger tens to hundreds of tool calls and run for minutes to hours, prompt engineering (now agentic prompt engineering) becomes one of the highest-leverage skills an engineer can master.
core_concepts.dan_words: "The prompt is now the fundamental unit of engineering. And with agents, every prompt you create becomes a force multiplier. One well-crafted prompt can generate tens and hundreds of hours of productive work. One bad prompt compounds failure at the same rate."
core_concepts.misconception: That prompt engineering is a soft, throwaway skill. Dan's rebuttal: it was 'once mocked as a joke,' but with agents it is now one of the most important skills for engineers to focus on and master.

core_concepts.name: The Stakeholder Trifecta (you / your team / your agents)
core_concepts.plain_english: You are not writing prompts only for yourself anymore. Three stakeholders read every prompt — you, your team, and your agents — and the winning move is a library of reusable, battle-tested prompts whose sections communicate clearly to all three. Consistency is what makes that communication cheap.
core_concepts.dan_words: "What we're doing here is learning how to best communicate what we want to the trifecta, you, your team, and your agents. Most importantly, your agents."
core_concepts.misconception: That prompts are private scratch work. In the age of agents a prompt is shared infrastructure with a brand-new consumer — the agent — so it must be engineered like any other interface.

core_concepts.name: Composable sections (swappable Lego blocks)
core_concepts.plain_english: An agentic prompt is assembled from a fixed vocabulary of ~13 named sections (Title, Purpose, Variables, Workflow, Report, Metadata, Instructions, Relevant Files, Codebase Structure, Expertise, Template, Examples, High Level Prompt). Each has a distinct capability. You only add the sections you need and swap them in and out like Lego blocks — that composability plus consistency is what makes prompts reusable.
core_concepts.dan_words: "The winners here are building libraries of reusable battle-tested agentic prompts with composable sections that work like lego blocks. You can swap these in and swap them out when and if you need them."
core_concepts.misconception: That you must use every section, or that section names are fixed law. You can name sections whatever you want; Dan uses 'the most consistent, the most information dense keywords.' The discipline is: only add what you need, and stay consistent.

core_concepts.name: The Seven Levels of Agentic Prompt Formats
core_concepts.plain_english: Seven prompt formats that stack on each other, each unlocking one new capability: (1) High Level Prompt, (2) Workflow Prompt, (3) Control Flow Prompt, (4) Delegate Prompt, (5) Higher Order Prompt, (6) Template Metaprompt, (7) Self-Improving Prompt. Every level inherits the sections of the levels below it and adds one. Levels 1-4 cover 80-90% of real engineering work; levels 5-7 are 'meta' territory (prompts that build and improve prompts).
core_concepts.dan_words: "All the prompts stack up on each other and the workflow prompt is an absolute pillar for all subsequent prompt levels... Levels one through let's say four will be 80 or 90% of all of your prompts."
core_concepts.misconception: That higher level = better. The right move is the lowest level that gets the job done — 'usually level three, level four is all you need.' You reach up only when the capability is required.

core_concepts.name: The Workflow section is the pillar
core_concepts.plain_english: The Workflow section — a sequential, numbered play of exactly what you want the agent to do — is the single most useful section (graded S-tier usefulness) and the one that maps directly onto a modern agentic tool's todo/plan list. Control flow, loops, and delegation all live inside the workflow. It is the backbone of every level from 2 upward.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Out of all the agentic prompt formats we'll look at, this is easily the most important one. Why is that? It's because of this workflow section... The most important section you'll write is the workflow."
core_concepts.misconception: That the flashy meta-prompt levels matter most. Dan says it over and over: 90% of the time all you need is a great workflow section at level three or four.

core_concepts.name: Input → Workflow → Output framework
core_concepts.plain_english: A consistent three-step way to design any prompt: Inputs (Variables) → the actual Work (Workflow) → Output (Report). The input and output are especially for you and your team (what comes in, what goes out); the workflow is where the agent does the engineering. Use this frame to design prompts fast and predictably.
core_concepts.dan_words: "It has the inputs, it has the workflow and it has the output, input, workflow, output. This is a very consistent three-step pattern you can use to think about how to design and build your prompts."
core_concepts.misconception: That every prompt needs all three. If you don't care about output format, drop Report; if nothing is passed in, drop Variables. The frame is a design lens, not a mandatory template.

core_concepts.name: Static vs dynamic variables
core_concepts.plain_english: Dynamic variables accept input at runtime via Claude Code's argument syntax ($1, $2, $ARGUMENTS) and change every run (e.g. USER_PROMPT: $1). Static variables are fixed values written into the prompt that you reference throughout and change in one place (e.g. PLAN_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY: `specs/`). Both use a consistent NAME: value syntax in a Variables section, referenced by name across the prompt so a single edit propagates everywhere.
core_concepts.dan_words: "This is a static variable... a variable we're placing right in the prompt that doesn't change... versus a the user prompt, a dynamic variable, right? That changes as you pass in work... Notice how much time I'm saving by having just a single static variable here that we can reference throughout the prompt."
core_concepts.misconception: That variables need a special templating engine. It's natural-language convention — a consistent NAME: value syntax the model is powerful enough to resolve wherever it's referenced. (Dynamic variables come first, static second; prefer $1/$2 over $ARGUMENTS for multiple args.)

core_concepts.name: Delegation — a prompt that writes prompts for sub-agents
core_concepts.plain_english: A Level-4 delegate prompt makes your primary agent the prompt engineer for its sub-agents: it designs detailed, self-contained prompts, defines clear output expectations, and fires N agents in parallel (Task tool) or a background CLI instance. Because LLMs are non-deterministic, spinning up multiple agents on different aspects of a problem returns diverse results. This is the 'D' (Delegate) of the R&D context-engineering framework from AH-1.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Our primary agent is instructing the sub agents... Our primary agent is the prompt engineer for our sub agents. And this is where things get really tricky... we're writing prompts that write prompts."
core_concepts.misconception: That delegation is just 'more prompting.' It's structurally harder (S-tier usefulness, A-tier skill): you must consciously manage the flow of information between agents, because a stateless sub-agent only knows the self-contained prompt you hand it.

core_concepts.name: Template Metaprompt — the prompt that builds prompts
core_concepts.plain_english: A Level-6 prompt whose Template section (a.k.a. Specified Format) encodes the exact output structure you want a NEW prompt to have, so the agent fills in the blanks and generates a well-formed prompt in your house style. Paired with a Documentation section (a context map the agent web-fetches first), it teaches your agent to build prompts like you and your team build them. This is the peak-leverage skill: once you can generate prompts, your agentic engineering velocity scales hard.
core_concepts.dan_words: "This is the most powerful prompt you can write. It's the prompt that creates your other prompts... once you unlock this S tier skill and usefulness level, these template meta prompts at level six, your agentic engineering velocity scales up very, very quickly."
core_concepts.misconception: That meta-prompting is a novelty. Dan frames it as the highest-ROI investment in the codebase: 'this will pay you back massive dividends for every prompt you write that you can have your agent create for you.'

core_concepts.name: Self-Improving Prompt — the agent that updates the agent
core_concepts.plain_english: A Level-7 (expert-level) prompt with a dynamic Expertise section that another prompt (or itself) updates with new knowledge over time. In the cc_hook_expert pattern, a dedicated _improve prompt reviews recent changes and rewrites ONLY the ## Expertise sections of the _plan and _build experts while leaving their Workflows stable — updating the context inside the prompt in a live way, so the expert grows more proficient in one narrow domain.
core_concepts.dan_words: "We're having our agents update our agents. How? By having our prompts update our prompts... We're basically updating the context inside of our prompts in a live way. You have self-updating prompts."
core_concepts.misconception: That every prompt should self-improve. These are rare — 'it's unlikely that you even have a use case.' The pattern works best when a SEPARATE prompt is dedicated to updating the expertise, and only the Expertise section is touched (workflows stay stable).

core_concepts.name: System prompts vs user prompts (scope & persistence)
core_concepts.plain_english: Every section graded in the tier list is for USER prompts — the prompts that flow into your context window (all your slash commands). System prompts are different: they set the rules for EVERY conversation, can't be changed mid-conversation, must handle many scenarios, and their mistakes scale to every user prompt. Written once, run many times. You append or overwrite them only when you build your own specialized agents (Claude Code SDK, AH-3). Best system-prompt sections: Purpose, Instructions, Examples (and a loose Workflow); avoid Variables, Report, Expertise, Templates, Metadata.
core_concepts.dan_words: "The big idea here with a system prompt versus a user prompt is the scope and level of persistence... System prompts are rules for all conversations... A bad system prompt is bad instructions for the whole job."
core_concepts.misconception: That the tier-list grades apply to system prompts too. They don't — they're graded for user prompts. System prompts are one to three orders of magnitude more consequential and demand far more delicacy; most engineers rarely reach that level.

core_concepts.name: Consistency is king
core_concepts.plain_english: The through-line of the whole lesson: reusing the same prompt format and the same interchangeable sections every time is what makes you (and your team and your agents) faster. Consistency is the greatest weapon against confusion. Boredom is the goal — a repetitive, predictable prompt structure means you spend zero cycles re-learning your own tools and can CRUD prompts at light speed.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Consistency is the greatest weapon against confusion for both you and your agent... consistency beats complexity, consistency makes you faster... Consistency is king when it comes to writing great agentic prompts."
core_concepts.misconception: That novelty or cleverness per prompt is good. Dan wants you 'annoyed and kind of bored of this workflow' — the sameness IS the feature; it's what lets one prompt (and ten more like it) be handed off without friction.

seven_levels.capability: Reusable, ad-hoc, static prompt — the one-off you throw in a file the moment you start repeating work an agent can do without a problem.
seven_levels.dan_note: A great place to start, a terrible place to end. 'Three times marks a pattern' — copy what you're doing and write it as a high level prompt, then move up.

seven_levels.capability: A sequential, numbered workflow with input → work → output. The biggest milestone; the Workflow section maps directly onto a modern tool's todo/plan list. Pillar for every level above.
seven_levels.dan_note: Easily the most important format because of the workflow section. This is where you get the majority of your prompt output.

seven_levels.capability: Adds conditionals, loops, and early returns inside the workflow (e.g. 'If no PATH_TO_PLAN, STOP and ask'; an <image-loop> XML block that repeats N times).
sections: ...all previous levels (control flow lives inside Workflow)
seven_levels.dan_note: About as powerful as, or a little more than, the workflow prompt — but more challenging, because you must reason through the control flow the workflow works through.

seven_levels.capability: Kicks off other agents (parallel sub-agents via Task, or a background CLI instance). Your primary agent becomes the prompt engineer for its sub-agents. The 'D' of R&D context engineering.
sections: Variables w/ agent config (model, count, tools, etc.)
seven_levels.dan_note: Ultra useful, hard to use — you're managing multiple agent instances and writing prompts that write prompts. You must be conscious of the flow of information between agents. 'This is the future of engineering.'

seven_levels.capability: Accepts another reusable prompt (a file/plan) as input. Provides a consistent top-level structure so the lower-level prompt passed in can change while the scaffolding stays the same. Prompts passed into prompts.
seven_levels.dan_note: The most obvious one: the prompt that builds work into your codebase based on a plan you pass in (e.g. /build specs/thing.md, where the plan comes from /quick-plan or an expert).

seven_levels.capability: A prompt used to create a NEW prompt in a specific, dynamic format. Its Template (Specified Format) section encodes the exact output structure; the agent fills in the blanks. Teaches your agent to build prompts like you build them.
seven_levels.dan_note: The most powerful prompt you can write — the prompt that creates your other prompts. The peak of agentic prompt engineering; unlocking it scales your velocity dramatically.

seven_levels.capability: A prompt updated by itself or another prompt/agent with new information, via a dynamic Expertise section. The agent that updates the agent. Rare, advanced, domain-narrow.
seven_levels.dan_note: Expert level. Best pattern: a separate _improve prompt updates ONLY the ## Expertise sections and leaves the Workflow stable. 'These prompts are absolutely insane' when you have the use case.

sections_catalog.note: Definitive list of the gradable section entities from apps/prompt_tier_list/src/constants/entities.ts (13 sections). Tier = usefulness/skill as placed on-screen in the final grid at ~45:40. Axes: usefulness S(top)→D(bottom); skill D=Beginner(left)→S=Expert(right).

sections.name: # Title
sections.purpose: Names the prompt with a clear, action-oriented H1. Immediately communicates what the prompt does.

sections.name: ## High Level Prompt
sections.purpose: A high-level, detail-void description of what you want the agent to do. The required core of a Level-1 prompt. Very easy to write; decent value with almost no effort.

sections.name: ## Metadata
sections.purpose: YAML frontmatter for Claude Code: allowed-tools, description, argument-hint, optional model. Lets you pin exact tools/models; otherwise not hugely valuable. Other tools have their own version.

sections.name: ## Purpose
sections.purpose: One or two sentences of direct, agent-directed language stating exactly what this prompt is meant to do. Powerful and simple; sets the tone of voice ('talk to your agent').

sections.name: ## Variables
sections.purpose: Dynamic ($1/$2/$ARGUMENTS) and static (fixed) values in a consistent NAME: value syntax, referenced by name throughout. Where prompts become massively more reusable.

sections.name: ## Instructions
sections.purpose: A bullet list of auxiliary/guardrail information that aids the workflow. Distinct from Workflow (the play-by-play); more valuable in system prompts than user prompts. Often you can skip it.

sections.name: ## Relevant Files
sections.purpose: A specific set of files for the agent to reference — speeds it up, gives it a quick way to find existing files. Like Codebase Structure but a flat file set. Not a game-breaker.

sections.name: ## Codebase Structure
sections.purpose: A context map: a tree of where files are and what they do at a 100-foot view. You do NOT tell the agent to read them — you give it a map so it finds relevant files fast without burning tokens on search.

sections.name: ## Workflow
sections.purpose: The sequential, numbered step-by-step play of exactly what the agent should do. THE most useful section. Maps to the agent's todo/plan list. Hosts control flow, loops, and delegation.

sections.name: ## Expertise
sections.purpose: Accumulated domain knowledge, patterns, and standards embedded in the prompt — the section that makes a prompt self-improving (Level 7). Works best when a separate prompt updates it.

sections.name: ## Template
sections.purpose: The exact output structure (a.k.a. Specified Format / Plan Format) the agent should generate, with <placeholder> blocks it fills in. The heart of a Template Metaprompt (Level 6). Very powerful, very hard.

sections.name: ## Examples
sections.purpose: Concrete demonstrations of the desired output/result. Can drastically increase agent performance; doesn't take much skill to write.

sections.name: ## Report
sections.purpose: The output/format section: how the agent responds — JSON, YAML, a specific structure, or required fields. Distinct from a bare Response; controls what comes back.

axes.x_skill: Left→right = Beginner (D) to Expert (S): how much skill the section/format takes to operate.
axes.y_usefulness: Top→bottom = Useful (S) to Useless (D): how valuable the section/format is.

tier_list.grid_source: Final on-screen grid at ~45:40 in the video (frame t2740-final-tier-list.jpg). Every position below was cross-verified against Dan's spoken grade at the moment he placed it.
tier_list.headline_reading: The single most useful section (Workflow) is only C-skill to operate — high value, low cost, which is why Dan says 90% of the time all you need is a great workflow at level 3-4. The peak-leverage cell (S/S) holds template_metaprompt.md and the ## Template section: maximum usefulness AND maximum skill.

input_workflow_output.framework: Every well-built prompt can be read as Input → Workflow → Output.
input_workflow_output.input: Variables — what comes in (dynamic + static). Especially for you and your team.
input_workflow_output.workflow: The actual engineering work the agent performs. The pillar section.
input_workflow_output.output: Report — what goes out, in the format you specify. Especially for you and your team.
input_workflow_output.dan_note: The input and output are specifically useful for you and your team; the workflow is where the agent does the work. Use it as a design lens; drop any of the three you don't need.

system_vs_user_prompts.everything_graded_is_user_prompts: Every section in the tier list is graded for USER prompts — all your Claude Code slash commands go into the context window as user prompts.
system_vs_user_prompts.system_prompt_definition: Rules for all conversations; the AI's personality + rulebook. Written once, run many times. Can't change mid-conversation, must handle many scenarios, and mistakes scale to every user prompt — so ~1-3 orders of magnitude more consequential.
system_vs_user_prompts.where_you_touch_them: Rarely. You append (background.md uses --append-system-prompt) or overwrite (Claude Code SDK, AH-3) system prompts only when you build your own specialized agents. Sub-agents (e.g. docs-scraper.md) ARE system prompts.
best_sections_for_system_prompts: Workflow — usually too specific, but allowed as a LOOSE structure (workflows reduce agency to increase determinism)
system_vs_user_prompts.count_in_codebase: Only ~4 system prompts in the whole repo: the background prompt's appended system prompt, plus the sub-agent definitions in .claude/agents/ (docs-scraper, meta-agent, crypto-coin-analyzer).

step_by_step_demo: (0:47) Intro slide 'The Stakeholder Trifecta' — You / Your Team / Your Agents — the mindset shift that frames the lesson.
(3:56-4:15) Level 1 High Level Prompt. Open all_tools.md: two sections (Title + high-level prompt) that ask the agent to read its system prompt and list all tools. Runs in any chat interface.
(5:00-6:23) Open start.md (Title + Purpose + high-level prompt with cd/bun install/bun run dev steps). Grade Title (C useful / D skill), High Level Prompt & Purpose (B / D) on the tier-list app.
(6:38-8:18) Level 2 Workflow Prompt — 'a huge milestone.' Grade the Workflow section S-useful / C-skill and the workflow_prompt.md format A / C.
(7:34) Open prime.md: description metadata, # Prime, Purpose, ## Workflow (git ls-files; read README.md), ## Report. The most basic workflow prompt; grade Metadata (C/C) and Report.

(9:30-11:30) Open build.md and quick-plan.md. Introduce Variables (build's PATH_TO_PLAN: $ARGUMENTS dynamic; quick-plan's USER_PROMPT: $1 dynamic + PLAN_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY: `specs/` static) and the Instructions section. Grade Variables A/B, Instructions ~B/C.

(11:30-19:20) Open prime_tier_list.md: no metadata; Title + Purpose + ## Codebase Structure (a context map — 'take note but do not read') + a richer Workflow ('read these files exclusively', IMPORTANT keyword) + Report. Grade Codebase Structure C/C. Establish Input → Workflow → Output.

(20:33-24:30) Level 3 Control Flow. build.md line 17 ('If no PATH_TO_PLAN, STOP immediately and ask') = early return. create_image.md: prerequisite STOP conditionals + an <image-loop> XML block (loop N images). edit_image.md: loop + conditionals, no Report. Grade control_flow_prompt.md A/B.

(26:17-34:00) Level 4 Delegate. parallel_subagents.md (PROMPT_REQUEST $1, COUNT $2; primary agent designs self-contained sub-agent prompts, fires N via Task) — Dan runs it live at count=5 to append to CLAUDE.md. load_ai_docs.md loops URLs and calls @agent-docs-scraper (5 doc scrapers run). background.md fires a full Claude Code CLI instance with --append-system-prompt + run_in_background. Grade delegate_prompt.md S/A.

(34:54-35:40) Level 5 Higher Order. Reopen build.md: the key is passing a plan (a prompt/file) IN as a variable while the top-level structure stays constant. Grade higher_order_prompt.md B-useful / A-skill.

(36:52-42:00) Level 6 Template Metaprompt. t_metaprompt_workflow.md: HIGH_LEVEL_PROMPT in; a Documentation context map (web-fetched first); a ## Specified Format template the agent fills in to emit a new prompt. plan_vite_vue.md: a rapid-prototyping meta prompt with Codebase Structure + a big Plan Format template. Grade template_metaprompt.md S/S and the Template section S/S.

(42:14-44:00) Level 7 Self-Improving. cc_hook_expert_plan.md with a dynamic ## Expertise section (hook file-structure, event knowledge, patterns); cc_hook_expert_improve.md updates ONLY that Expertise. Grade Expertise A/A and self_improving_prompt.md A/S.
(44:23-45:40) Place the last two sections — Examples (A/B, 'right below variables') and Relevant Files (C/C) — completing the AGENTIC PROMPT TIER LIST grid. This is the money-shot frame.

(46:33-55:00) System prompts vs user prompts: scope & persistence; everything graded was user prompts; background.md's appended system prompt and the docs-scraper sub-agent as concrete system-prompt examples; which sections work for system prompts (Purpose/Instructions/Examples, loose Workflow).

(55:36-end) Next move: finish TAC first, then AH-3 (Claude Code SDK / build domain-specific agents with custom system prompts). Start at Level 1, scale to the Workflow Prompt, stack up to the Template Metaprompt.

prerequisites_tools: Claude Code (the primary agentic coding tool used throughout)
Bun (runs the prompt_tier_list Vite + Vue 3 app: bun install / bun run dev)
Optional for the image prompts: a Replicate API token (REPLICATE_API_TOKEN) + the Replicate MCP server or curl/jq/base64
Optional for load_ai_docs: the Firecrawl MCP server (falls back to WebFetch)
An IDE (Dan uses VS Code; the 'collapse to H2' review workflow relies on editor folding)
Recommended prior lessons: finish TAC (esp. ZTE / AFK / ADWs) and AH-1 (R&D framework / elite context engineering)
what_student_must_internalize: The prompt is the fundamental unit of engineering; agentic prompt engineering is now a top-tier skill, not a joke.
You write for the stakeholder trifecta — you, your team, your agents — most importantly your agents.
There are ~13 named, swappable sections and 7 stacking levels; add only the sections you need and reach for the lowest level that does the job (usually 3-4).
The Workflow section is the pillar: S-tier usefulness, only C-tier skill. Master it before anything meta.
Design with Input → Workflow → Output; use static vs dynamic variables to make one edit propagate everywhere.
Delegation (L4) makes your primary agent the prompt engineer for its sub-agents; you must manage information flow between agents.
The peak-leverage move is the Template Metaprompt (L6) — the prompt that writes your prompts — followed by the Self-Improving Prompt (L7), which updates only its Expertise.
Every grade in the tier list is for USER prompts. System prompts are different in scope and persistence and demand far more care.
Consistency is king: boring, repeatable prompt structure is the feature — it's what lets you CRUD reusable prompts at light speed and hand work off to compute.
common_weak_student_failures: Chasing the meta levels (6-7) first because they sound powerful, and never mastering the Workflow section that does 90% of real work.
Treating section names as sacred law (or thinking you must use all of them) instead of learning the underlying capabilities and adding only what's needed.
Confusing the Workflow section (the step-by-step play) with the Instructions section (auxiliary guardrails) — or the Codebase Structure map (don't read) with Relevant Files (do read).
Writing every value inline instead of extracting a static variable, then editing the same path in ten places when it changes.
Assuming the tier-list grades apply to system prompts — they're for USER prompts only; system prompts are a different, higher-stakes game.
Building a self-improving prompt with no real use case, or letting the _improve step rewrite the Workflow (it must touch ONLY the Expertise section).
Changing the prompt format every time (novelty), which forces you, your team, and your agents to re-learn structure on every read and defeats reuse.
In delegation, handing a sub-agent an under-specified prompt — sub-agents are stateless and only know the self-contained prompt you design for them.
teach_back_prompt: Without notes, explain to a colleague: (1) why the prompt is now 'the fundamental unit of engineering' and who the stakeholder trifecta is; (2) name the seven levels in order and the ONE capability each adds, then justify why the Workflow section is graded most useful yet only mid-skill; (3) give a real static-variable and a real dynamic-variable from the codebase and say why the distinction saves time; (4) describe how a Level-6 Template Metaprompt differs from a Level-7 Self-Improving Prompt, using cc_hook_expert as your example; and (5) explain why every grade in the tier list is for USER prompts and what changes when you move to a SYSTEM prompt. Finish by resolving the paradox: why is being 'bored' by your own consistent prompt format a sign you're doing it right?

retrieval_questions.q: Who are the three stakeholders every agentic prompt is written for, and which matters most?
retrieval_questions.a: You, your team, and your agents — the stakeholder trifecta. Your agents matter most (they execute the tool chains), though the point is clear communication to all three.

retrieval_questions.q: Name the seven levels in order and the one capability each adds.
retrieval_questions.a: 1 High Level Prompt (reusable ad-hoc one-off), 2 Workflow Prompt (sequential input→work→output), 3 Control Flow Prompt (conditions/loops/early returns), 4 Delegate Prompt (fires other agents), 5 Higher Order Prompt (accepts another prompt/file as input), 6 Template Metaprompt (writes a new prompt in a set format), 7 Self-Improving Prompt (updates its own Expertise).

retrieval_questions.q: Which section is graded most useful, and what is its skill grade?
retrieval_questions.a: The Workflow section — S-tier usefulness, only C-tier skill. It maps onto the agent's todo/plan list and hosts control flow, loops, and delegation.

retrieval_questions.q: What is the difference between a static and a dynamic variable? Give an example of each.
retrieval_questions.a: Dynamic variables take runtime input via $1/$2/$ARGUMENTS and change each run (e.g. USER_PROMPT: $1). Static variables are fixed values referenced throughout that you change in one place (e.g. PLAN_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY: `specs/`).

retrieval_questions.q: What is the Input → Workflow → Output framework, and which parts serve you/your team?
retrieval_questions.a: Variables (input) → Workflow (the work) → Report (output). Input and output are especially for you and your team; the workflow is where the agent does the engineering.

retrieval_questions.q: In a delegation prompt, what role does the primary agent play toward its sub-agents?
retrieval_questions.a: It becomes the prompt engineer for its sub-agents — designing detailed, self-contained prompts with clear output expectations, since sub-agents are stateless.

retrieval_questions.q: What makes a Level-7 self-improving prompt work, and what must the _improve step NOT touch?
retrieval_questions.a: A dynamic Expertise section updated by a separate prompt/agent over time. The _improve step updates ONLY the ## Expertise sections and must leave the Workflow stable.

retrieval_questions.q: How does a Template Metaprompt (L6) differ from a Higher Order Prompt (L5)?
retrieval_questions.a: A Higher Order prompt (L5) accepts an existing prompt/plan file as input and runs it. A Template Metaprompt (L6) generates a brand-new prompt in a specified format the agent fills in — it builds prompts rather than consuming them.

retrieval_questions.q: Every section grade in the tier list applies to which kind of prompt?
retrieval_questions.a: User prompts. All Claude Code slash commands enter the context window as user prompts. System prompts are graded/handled differently.

retrieval_questions.q: Name three sections that work well in a system prompt and three that don't.
retrieval_questions.a: Good: Purpose, Instructions, Examples (plus a loose Workflow). Avoid: Variables, Report, Expertise/Templates, Metadata/Relevant Files/Codebase Structure.

retrieval_questions.q: What is Dan's coworker test for prompt quality?
retrieval_questions.a: 'If I handed this to a coworker, could they complete this work top to bottom?' If yes, you've probably written a high-quality prompt.

retrieval_questions.q: Why does Dan want you 'bored' of the prompt workflow?
retrieval_questions.a: Because consistency is king — a repetitive, predictable format is the feature. It reduces confusion for you, your team, and your agents and lets you reuse and hand off prompts without friction.

current_practice_gaps.gap: Reusable expertise now ships as first-class Agent Skills (SKILL.md), not only slash commands
current_practice_gaps.why: The lesson encodes reusable prompts as .claude/commands/*.md slash commands and reusable behavior as sub-agents. Modern Claude Code adds Agent Skills — SKILL.md with frontmatter, progressive disclosure, and on-demand discovery — as the current idiom for packaging reusable engineering so it's discoverable and shareable. The seven-levels vocabulary maps 1:1 onto Skill bodies; the packaging has upgraded. The 'self-improving Expertise' idea also overlaps with today's memory/knowledge-file patterns.

current_practice_gaps.gap: Course-era model ids are pinned in metadata (claude-opus-4-1-20250805)
current_practice_gaps.why: quick-plan.md and background.md hard-code model: claude-opus-4-1-20250805, and the README aliases/metaprompt default to sonnet/opus generically. Current model families have moved on (Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5, Haiku 4.5, Fable 5). The Metadata section's model field is exactly where you'd swap these; treat pinned ids as period detail and pick the current best model at run time.

current_practice_gaps.gap: Background/headless delegation has hardened into the Claude Agent SDK + richer headless flags
current_practice_gaps.why: background.md shells out to `claude --print --append-system-prompt … --dangerously-skip-permissions --output-format text` with run_in_background. That still works and is the clearest teaching form, but production delegation now uses the Claude Agent SDK (Python/TypeScript), structured --output-format json/stream-json, session resume, permission modes, and typed hooks — which is exactly what AH-3 (Claude Code SDK) builds toward. Same concept (agent as callable component, append vs overwrite system prompt), richer machinery.
current_practice_gaps.yt_topic: Claude Code SDK / headless agents / building your own agent

current_practice_gaps.gap: Parallel delegation now has worktree isolation and first-class background tasks
current_practice_gaps.why: parallel_subagents.md fires N Task sub-agents in one batch — still valid — but current practice adds git-worktree isolation for agents that mutate files concurrently, plus background task orchestration and multi-agent workflow tooling. A modern reader should know the delegation ceiling is far higher (dozens of isolated agents) than the single-batch Task fan-out shown here. AH-4 (the O-agent / multi-agent orchestration) scales exactly this.

current_practice_gaps.gap: Doc-scraping via Firecrawl MCP is one option among several context-loading patterns
current_practice_gaps.why: load_ai_docs.md depends on the Firecrawl MCP server (with a WebFetch fallback). Current Claude Code has broader native web tooling and MCP options, and the 'load docs into ai_docs/ for agents to read' pattern is one instance of the R&D (Reduce/Delegate) context engineering from AH-1. Concept is durable; the specific MCP dependency and the 24-hour TTL are implementation detail.
